tip: Hindi builds the passive with जाना (jana = to go): बनाया गया था (banaya gaya tha = was built) is literally 'built went was'. The 'go' verb, not 'be', is what makes it passive.
बनाई जा रही है (banai ja rahi hai = is being built) is feminine throughout to match सड़क (sadak = road) – both parts of a Hindi passive agree with the subject.
No one says who considers: मानते हैं (maante hain = [people] consider) has no subject at all. Where English says 'is considered', Hindi often just drops the 'they'.
द्वारा (dwara = by) marks who did it: पुलिस द्वारा (pulis dwara = by the police). It's formal, news-report Hindi – everyday speech usually just doesn't name the doer.
English makes 'students' the subject of 'were given'. Hindi doesn't: छात्रों को (chhatron ko = to the students) stays, and दी गई (di gai) agrees with वर्दी (vardi = uniform).
बनवाया (banvaya) is not plain 'built' – the -वा- (-va-) means the Mughals had it built by others. बनाया (banaya) = built it yourself; बनवाया = got it built.
बनी है (bani hai) is not a passive – it's बनना (banna = to get made). Hindi often says 'the library became' where English needs 'was built', no जाना (jana) involved.
A sentence is announced aloud in Hindi: सज़ा सुनाई गई (saza sunai gai) is literally 'the punishment was made heard' – सुनाना (sunana) means to make someone hear.
जाने से मना है (jane se mana hai) is literally 'there is refusal from going' – the banned action takes से (se = from). That's the standard 'not allowed' pattern on signs.
One English word, three Hindi verbs: रद्द कर दी गई (radd kar di gai = was cancelled) stacks do + give + go. The compound कर देना (kar dena) survives inside the passive.
There's no word for 'as': सर्वश्रेष्ठ खिलाड़ी चुना गया (sarvashreshth khiladi chuna gaya) is just 'best player was chosen' – the role sits bare next to the verb.
